meta.provenance: Authored from model knowledge (cutoff Jan 2026). Original explanations. Shortcuts/editor locations are factual data.

commands.name: Fly Navigation (WASD)
commands.description: Hold the right mouse button and use WASD (plus Q and E for down and up) to fly through the level like a game camera. It is the fundamental way to move through an archviz scene, and scrolling the wheel while holding RMB changes flight speed on the fly.

commands.name: Orbit Navigation
commands.description: Holding Alt with the left mouse button orbits the camera around its pivot, while Alt with the right button dollies in and out and Alt with the middle button pans. This Maya-style scheme suits object inspection, such as circling a facade module or a piece of joinery.

commands.name: Focus Selected
commands.description: Frames the selected actor in the viewport and re-centres the orbit pivot on it. Pressing F before orbiting is the habit that makes navigation predictable in large architectural levels, where the pivot otherwise drifts far from your subject.

commands.name: Camera Bookmarks
commands.description: Stores up to ten viewport camera positions per level, set with Ctrl plus a number and recalled with the number alone. Bookmarking key views such as the entrance approach, atrium and roof terrace makes design reviews and repeat screenshots dramatically faster.

commands.name: Game View
commands.description: Toggles off all editor-only visuals such as icons, gizmos and volume outlines, showing the scene exactly as a player or client would see it. Flick it on whenever you judge composition or lighting, because sprite clutter badly distorts a reading of the image.

commands.name: Immersive Mode
commands.description: Expands the active viewport to fill the entire window, hiding panels and toolbars. Combined with Game View it turns the editor into a clean full-screen presentation surface for live walkthroughs with clients.

commands.name: Camera Speed
commands.description: Adjusts how fast the fly camera moves, via the speed control in the viewport toolbar or by scrolling while navigating. Matching speed to context, slow for interiors and fast for masterplans, is a small habit that saves constant frustration.

commands.name: Pilot Actor
commands.description: Locks the viewport to a selected camera or light so that flying the viewport moves that actor directly. Piloting a Cine Camera is the natural way to compose shots, and piloting a directional light lets you drag the sun by eye until shadows fall where you want them.

commands.name: Viewport View Modes
commands.shortcut: Alt+2 wireframe, Alt+3 unlit, Alt+4 lit
commands.description: Switches the viewport between Lit, Unlit, Wireframe and diagnostic modes such as Detail Lighting. Unlit is invaluable for checking texture work without lighting influence, while wireframe exposes the density of imported CAD geometry.

commands.name: Orthographic Views
commands.shortcut: Alt+G perspective, Alt+H front, Alt+J top, Alt+K left
commands.description: Switches the viewport between perspective and true orthographic projections such as top, front and side. Architects find the top view especially useful for laying out furniture and site elements with drawing-like precision.

commands.name: Select Tool
commands.description: Switches to plain selection with no transform gizmo active, reducing the risk of accidentally dragging actors while reviewing a scene. Marquee-drag selects multiple actors, and Ctrl-click adds or removes from the selection.

commands.name: Move Tool
commands.description: Activates the translation gizmo for dragging actors along axes or planes, with exact values editable in the Details panel. Everyday archviz use ranges from placing furniture to shifting whole context blocks into alignment with a site survey.

commands.name: Rotate Tool
commands.description: Activates the rotation gizmo for turning actors about any axis, honouring the current angle snap increment. Rotating entourage such as chairs, cars and trees away from identical orientations is a quick realism win in populated scenes.

commands.name: Scale Tool
commands.description: Activates the scale gizmo for uniform or per-axis resizing of actors. Slight random scaling across repeated vegetation and props breaks up the cloned look, though architectural elements should generally stay at true size.

commands.name: World / Local Transform Space
commands.description: Toggles the gizmo between world axes and the actor's own local axes via the globe icon in the viewport toolbar. Local space is essential when sliding an object along its own length, for example moving a rotated partition wall along its face rather than along world X.

commands.name: Grid Snapping
commands.description: Constrains translation to fixed increments set in the viewport toolbar, keeping placement tidy and modular. Matching the snap value to your project module, say 100 mm for interiors, gives CAD-like discipline when assembling repeated architectural components.

commands.name: Rotation Snapping
commands.description: Limits rotation to fixed angular steps such as 5, 10 or 90 degrees. Keep it on for orthogonal building work, and drop to small increments or off entirely when naturalistically scattering planting and loose props.

commands.name: Duplicate (Alt+Drag)
commands.description: Holding Alt while dragging a transform gizmo leaves the original in place and moves a fresh copy, effectively duplicating and positioning in one gesture. With grid snapping enabled it is the fastest way to run out rows of columns, luminaires or facade bays.

commands.name: Duplicate Actor
commands.description: Duplicates the selected actors in place, ready to be repositioned. Unlike Alt-drag it needs no gizmo movement, which suits duplicating something you intend to move numerically in the Details panel instead.

commands.name: Snap to Floor
commands.description: Drops the selected actor straight down until it rests on the surface below. Indispensable when set-dressing, since furniture, people and planting placed from the library rarely land exactly on the finished floor level.

commands.name: Delete Actor
commands.description: Removes the selected actors from the level. Note that deleting from the level does not remove the underlying asset from the Content Browser, so the project itself is unaffected.

commands.name: Details Panel Transforms
commands.description: Edits an actor's location, rotation and scale numerically, alongside every other exposed property such as mobility and materials. Typing exact coordinates is how imported survey or setting-out information is respected rather than eyeballed.

commands.name: Open Content Browser
commands.description: Summons the Content Browser, the file manager for every asset in the project: meshes, materials, textures, Blueprints and levels. Ctrl+Space opens it as an overlay, keeping the viewport large until you actually need to browse.

commands.name: Import Assets
commands.description: Brings external files such as FBX meshes, textures and audio into the project, with per-import options for scale, materials and collision. For architectural geometry, Datasmith import is usually preferable to raw FBX because it preserves scene structure and instancing.

commands.name: Create Folder
commands.description: Adds a folder to the project's content tree, the basis of a disciplined asset structure. A predictable scheme, for instance separating architecture, entourage, materials and media, pays off enormously once a project accumulates thousands of assets.

commands.name: Asset Search and Filters
commands.description: Finds assets by name and narrows the view with type filters such as Static Mesh, Material Instance or Level Sequence. Filtering by type is often faster than folder navigation when hunting one texture among a large imported Datasmith set.

commands.name: Migrate Assets
commands.description: Copies selected assets and every dependency they reference into another project's Content folder in one operation. It is how a practice moves a proven furniture pack, material library or lighting rig between archviz projects without broken references.

commands.name: Fix Up Redirectors
commands.description: Cleans up the invisible redirector files Unreal leaves behind after assets are moved or renamed, repointing every reference to the new location. Running it after reorganising folders prevents the classic problem of phantom assets and confusing duplicate paths.

commands.name: Reference Viewer
commands.description: Opens a node graph showing everything a selected asset references and everything that references it. Before deleting a material or mesh from a long-running archviz project, the Reference Viewer tells you exactly what would break.

commands.name: Save All
commands.description: Saves the current level and every modified asset in one action. Unreal keeps unsaved changes in memory per asset, so regular Save All is the habit that protects hours of material tweaking from a crash.

commands.name: Fab and Quixel Megascans
commands.description: Browses Epic's Fab marketplace, including the Megascans library of scanned surfaces, plants and props, and drops assets straight into the project. Scanned brick, asphalt and foliage are staples of photoreal archviz because their imperfection is real rather than authored.

commands.name: Place Actors Panel
commands.description: A palette of common actors, including lights, volumes, cameras and basic shapes, that you drag directly into the level. It is the quickest source for one-off items such as a Post Process Volume or a Player Start without hunting through menus.

commands.name: Group Actors
commands.description: Binds selected actors into a group that selects and transforms as one, with Shift+G to ungroup. Grouping a dining setting or a planted bed lets you reposition the whole arrangement repeatedly without re-selecting its parts.

commands.name: Attach Actor
commands.description: Parents one actor to another by dragging it onto the parent in the Outliner, so the child follows the parent's transforms. Attach light fittings to their pendant meshes, or door leaves to frames, and moving the parent keeps everything correctly assembled.

commands.name: Outliner Folders
commands.description: Organises the level's actor list into named folders, such as Structure, Glazing, Landscape and Entourage, with visibility toggles per folder. A structured Outliner is what keeps thousand-actor architectural levels navigable months into a project.

commands.name: Layers Panel
commands.description: Assigns actors to named layers that can be selected or hidden en masse, independent of the Outliner hierarchy. Layers suit cross-cutting sets like design options or all-glazing, echoing the layer discipline architects already know from CAD.

commands.name: Hide Actors
commands.description: Temporarily hides the selected actors in the editor viewport, with Ctrl+H restoring everything. Use it to peel away roofs and slabs while working inside a building, remembering that editor hiding does not affect what renders in game view or output.

commands.name: Hierarchical LOD (HLOD)
commands.description: Merges clusters of distant actors into simplified proxy meshes that swap in beyond a set distance, cutting draw calls dramatically. Large masterplan scenes with repeated context housing benefit most, keeping frame rates presentable on modest hardware.

commands.name: World Partition
commands.description: UE5's system for dividing a large level into a grid of cells that stream in and out automatically as the camera moves. City-scale masterplans and long linear infrastructure sites become workable because only the area around the viewer is loaded at once.

commands.name: Datasmith Import
commands.description: Imports a .udatasmith export from Revit, Archicad, Rhino, SketchUp, 3ds Max or Navisworks with hierarchy, materials, metadata and instancing intact. It is the backbone of the CAD-and-BIM-to-Unreal archviz pipeline, and BIM metadata survives for later querying or Blueprint logic.

commands.name: Datasmith Direct Link
commands.description: Maintains a live connection between a running CAD or BIM session and the Unreal Editor, pushing model updates without exporting files. During design development this shrinks the change-review loop from an export-import cycle to a single synchronise click.

commands.name: Datasmith Reimport
commands.description: Refreshes a previously imported Datasmith scene from an updated source file, applying geometry changes while respecting overrides you have made in Unreal. This keeps material polish and lighting work alive across design revisions instead of restarting each time.

commands.name: Enable Plugins
commands.description: The Edit > Plugins window switches optional engine features on and off per project. Archviz work typically enables Datasmith importers, Movie Render Queue, Sun Position Calculator and HDRI Backdrop before anything else, each requiring an editor restart.

commands.name: Enter Modeling Mode
commands.description: Switches the editor into a full mesh-editing toolset for creating and modifying geometry without leaving Unreal, selected from the Modes dropdown. It is invaluable for patching gaps in imported CAD models, blocking out context massing and building simple site elements in place.

commands.name: Create Primitive Shapes
commands.description: Generates parametric boxes, cylinders, spheres and planes directly in the level with editable dimensions before committing. Perfect for quick massing studies, plinths, and stand-in context blocks that will later be replaced with detailed geometry.

commands.name: PolyModel Editing
commands.description: Direct polygon-level editing, extruding, insetting, cutting and offsetting faces of a mesh inside the editor. Use it to raise a parapet, punch a rooflight opening or extend a wall on imported geometry without a round trip to the modelling package.

commands.name: Boolean Operation
commands.description: Combines two meshes by union, subtraction or intersection, for example subtracting a box to carve a doorway through an imported solid wall. Booleans provide CAD-like edits directly on game meshes, though results benefit from a quick normals and UV check afterwards.

commands.name: Merge Meshes
commands.description: Combines several selected meshes into a single static mesh asset, reducing actor count and draw calls. Merging a finished piece of fixed joinery or a fully dressed balcony simplifies both the Outliner and runtime performance.

commands.name: Auto UV / UV Unwrap
commands.description: Generates or repairs texture coordinates on a mesh, using automatic unwrapping or box projection. Imported CAD geometry frequently arrives with poor or missing UVs, and fixing them is the difference between stretched smears and correctly coursing brickwork.

commands.name: Simplify Mesh
commands.description: Reduces a mesh's triangle count while preserving its silhouette as far as possible. Heavy survey scans and over-tessellated CAD exports, such as a chair with a million triangles, can be brought down to sensible budgets for smooth interactive walkthroughs.

commands.name: Create Material
commands.description: Creates a new material asset via the Content Browser right-click menu, opening the node-based Material Editor to define its look. In archviz practice a small set of master materials, for painted plaster, timber, metal and glass, typically parents everything else via instances.

commands.name: Create Material Instance
commands.description: Derives a lightweight child material from a parent, exposing only the parent's parameters, such as colour, roughness and texture maps, for quick editing without shader recompilation. Instances are how one oak master becomes light oak flooring, dark oak doors and smoked oak panelling in seconds.

commands.name: Material Parameters
commands.description: Converts constants in a material graph into named scalar, vector or texture parameters that instances can override. Well-chosen parameters, such as tint, roughness, UV scale and normal strength, are what make a master material genuinely reusable across a project.

commands.name: Apply Material to Actor
commands.description: Assigns a material by dragging it from the Content Browser onto a mesh in the viewport, or by setting the material slot in the Details panel. Slot-level assignment matters on architectural meshes, which often carry several slots, for frame, glazing and gaskets, on one object.

commands.name: Enable Nanite on a Mesh
commands.description: Turns on Nanite virtualised geometry for a static mesh, letting the engine render extremely dense models by streaming only the detail each pixel needs. Archviz teams enable it on heavy scanned assets and ornate architectural elements so full detail survives without manual LOD authoring.

commands.name: Directional Light
commands.description: The sun: a light whose parallel rays and rotation define the scene's primary shadows and warmth. In archviz its angle is usually set from real solar geometry or piloted by eye until shadows model the facade attractively, with intensity in physical lux-scale values.

commands.name: Sky Atmosphere
commands.description: A physically based sky model that computes realistic sky colour, horizon haze and aerial perspective from the directional light's angle. It gives dawn, noon and dusk their distinct characters automatically, which underpins convincing time-of-day studies.

commands.name: Sky Light
commands.description: Captures the sky and distant scene into ambient illumination, filling shadows with believable sky colour instead of flat black. Set to real-time capture alongside Lumen it keeps interiors naturally lit as the sun angle or weather mood changes.

commands.name: Rect Light
commands.description: A rectangular area light emitting soft, realistically spread illumination from a defined panel. It is the archviz workhorse for luminous ceilings, LED coves, backlit signage and the classic softbox glow placed just outside a window.

commands.name: Point and Spot Lights
commands.description: Point lights radiate in all directions while spot lights cast a controllable cone, together covering most artificial fittings from pendants to downlights. Both accept physical intensity units and IES photometric profiles, so a lighting design's specified fittings can be previewed faithfully.

commands.name: Environment Light Mixer
commands.description: A single panel, opened from Window > Env. Light Mixer, that creates and edits the sun, sky atmosphere, sky light, clouds and fog together. It is the quickest route to a complete, coherent daylight setup in a fresh archviz level.

commands.name: HDRI Backdrop
commands.description: Places a dome that projects a high dynamic range panorama as both backdrop and light source, with a ground projection so the model appears to sit within the photograph. It is the fastest way to drop a building study into a believable captured environment for product-style presentation.

commands.name: Sun Position Calculator
commands.description: Drives the directional light from real geographic and temporal data: latitude, longitude, date, time and north offset. This turns lighting from art direction into evidence, supporting accurate solar access and overshadowing studies for planning submissions.

commands.name: Lumen Global Illumination
commands.description: UE5's dynamic global illumination and reflection system, computing bounced light in real time with no baking step. For architects it means moving the sun or toggling a design option updates the entire light response instantly, which transforms live design review.

commands.name: Build Lighting
commands.description: Bakes static lighting into lightmaps using the CPU or GPU Lightmass solvers, launched from the main toolbar's Build menu. Although Lumen has made baking optional, baked lighting still suits locked-down scenes targeting maximum quality on weaker hardware, at the cost of long build times per iteration.

commands.name: Post Process Volume
commands.description: A volume that applies camera and image settings, exposure, white balance, bloom, colour grading, ambient occlusion and more, either within its bounds or scene-wide via Infinite Extent. Almost every archviz level carries one as the central place where the image's final look is tuned.

commands.name: Exposure Control
commands.description: Configures auto-exposure limits or locks exposure manually, usually inside a Post Process Volume or a Cine Camera. Clamping or fixing exposure stops the image pumping brighter and darker as the camera moves between a bright atrium and a dim corridor, a hallmark of uncontrolled walkthroughs.

commands.name: Create Level Sequence
commands.description: Creates a cinematic timeline asset where cameras, transforms, visibility and properties are animated against time. Level Sequences are the foundation of every rendered archviz film, from a single slow push-in to a full multi-shot marketing edit.

commands.name: Add Cine Camera Actor
commands.description: Adds a cinematic camera with real photographic controls: sensor size, focal length, aperture and focus distance. Archviz shots benefit directly from photographic discipline, for instance a 24 mm architectural exterior or an 85 mm detail study, and Sequencer can spawn and animate it per shot.

commands.name: Keyframe Properties
commands.description: Records values, such as camera transforms, focal length or an actor's visibility, at chosen frames, which Sequencer interpolates into animation. Enabling auto-key makes every viewport adjustment while scrubbing become a keyframe, a fast way to rough out a camera move.

commands.name: Camera Cuts Track
commands.description: Defines which camera is live at each point in the timeline, allowing a sequence to cut between multiple framed shots. It is how a two-minute marketing film assembles exterior approach, lobby reveal and roof terrace shots into one deliverable.

commands.name: Movie Render Queue
commands.description: Renders Level Sequences offline at maximum quality, with high sample counts, anti-aliasing refinement, high resolutions and image-sequence output formats. It is the standard final-frame pipeline for archviz films and stills, trading render time for quality well beyond real-time playback.

commands.name: High Resolution Screenshot
commands.description: Captures the current viewport at a multiple of screen resolution via the viewport options menu, producing print-ready stills without Sequencer setup. It is the quick route to a large one-off image of a bookmarked view for a report or board.

commands.name: Open Level Blueprint
commands.description: Opens the visual script attached to the current level, reached from the toolbar's Blueprints button. It is the natural home for level-specific interactivity in a presentation, such as key presses that toggle design options, swap seasons or teleport between flats.

commands.name: Create Blueprint Class
commands.description: Creates a reusable actor class combining components and visual-script logic, via the Content Browser right-click menu. Archviz staples include a door that opens on approach, a light fitting with a switchable state and a material-configurator kiosk, each built once and placed many times.

commands.name: Add Component
commands.description: Adds building blocks, static meshes, lights, triggers, audio and more, to a Blueprint class in its Components panel. A door Blueprint, for example, combines a frame mesh, a leaf mesh, a box trigger and a timeline into one self-contained placeable asset.

commands.name: Compile Blueprint
commands.description: Validates and builds the Blueprint's graph so changes take effect, with errors and warnings reported on the offending nodes. Compile early and often; a stale uncompiled Blueprint silently running old logic is a classic source of confusion in interactive presentations.

commands.name: Event BeginPlay
commands.description: The event node that fires once when the level or actor starts running, making it the standard entry point for setup logic. In archviz presentations it commonly initialises the starting design option, time of day and camera position before the client takes control.

commands.name: Branch Node
commands.description: The visual-scripting if-statement, routing execution down True or False paths based on a boolean input. Holding B and clicking in the graph places one instantly, and it underlies almost every toggle in a presentation, such as whether a design option is currently shown.

commands.name: Timeline Node
commands.description: Outputs a value that changes over a defined duration along editable curves, driving smooth animated transitions from Blueprint logic. It is the standard mechanism behind opening doors, fading between material options and easing a camera to a new viewpoint.

commands.name: Play In Editor
commands.description: Runs the level as an interactive experience directly in the editor, spawning the player at a Player Start or the camera position. It is how you test a client walkthrough exactly as it will be experienced, including collision, interactions and walking pace.

commands.name: Simulate
commands.description: Starts the game running while leaving you in the free editor camera rather than possessing a player. Useful for watching ambient systems, animated people, traffic, swaying vegetation, behave from any vantage point while still selecting and inspecting actors.

commands.name: Eject and Possess
commands.description: During a play session, F8 ejects you from the player pawn into the free editor camera, and pressing it again re-possesses. Ejecting mid-walkthrough to nudge a chair or tweak a light, then dropping straight back in, makes live polish sessions very fluid.

commands.name: Stop Play Session
commands.description: Ends the current play or simulate session and returns to editing. Any changes made to runtime actor state during play are discarded, which is worth remembering before spending effort adjusting things while playing rather than ejected.

commands.name: Open Console
commands.description: Opens the command console for typing engine commands and console variables, with auto-completion as you type. It is the gateway to quick diagnostics and quality tweaks, from frame-rate statistics to resolution scaling, without opening any settings menus.

commands.name: Stat FPS
commands.description: The console command `stat fps` overlays the current frame rate and frame time on the viewport. It is the first sanity check before a live client walkthrough, since anything much below 30 fps reads as uncomfortable on screen.

commands.name: Stat Unit
commands.description: The console command `stat unit` breaks frame time into game thread, render thread and GPU figures, revealing where a slow scene is actually bottlenecked. In archviz the GPU is usually the culprit, pointing towards lighter shadows, reflections or resolution rather than simpler logic.

commands.name: Screen Percentage (r.ScreenPercentage)
commands.description: The console variable `r.ScreenPercentage` renders internally at a fraction or multiple of output resolution, with upscaling filling the gap. Dropping to 70–80 per cent often rescues frame rate on laptop demos with modest visual cost, while values above 100 sharpen stills.

commands.name: Nanite Visualisation
commands.description: Viewport visualisation modes, under Show > Visualize > Nanite, that colour the scene by Nanite triangle clusters, overdraw and which meshes are Nanite-enabled. A quick pass tells you whether heavy imported assets are actually benefiting from virtualised geometry.

commands.name: Lumen Visualisation
commands.description: Debug views that display the Lumen scene, surface cache and global illumination in isolation. When an interior corner looks oddly dark or a mirror-like wall misbehaves, these views show whether Lumen's simplified scene representation is capturing the geometry properly.

commands.name: Landscape Sculpt
commands.description: Creates and shapes terrain with brush-based sculpt, smooth, flatten and ramp tools, or imports a heightmap for surveyed ground. Site topography, berms, swales and gentle falls around a building are modelled here rather than as static meshes.

commands.name: Landscape Paint
commands.description: Paints blended material layers, grass, gravel, tarmac, bare earth, across the terrain using weight maps. Landscape material layers can automatically spawn ground-cover meshes, so painting a grass layer can also populate it with actual blades.

commands.name: Foliage Paint
commands.description: Scatters instanced meshes, trees, shrubs, grasses, even repeated props, with a brush that randomises scale, rotation and density per species. Because instances render far more cheaply than individual actors, it is the correct tool for planting schemes of any real size.

commands.name: Erase Foliage
commands.description: Removes painted foliage instances within the brush, by holding Shift with the paint tool or using the erase tool directly. Clearing planting away from paths, terraces and the building footprint after a generous first pass is quicker than painting carefully from the start.

commands.name: World Settings
commands.description: Per-level configuration, opened from Window > World Settings, covering the game mode, Lightmass quality and world-scale options. Archviz uses include assigning a walkthrough game mode with a suitable pawn, and tuning static lighting quality for baked scenes.

commands.name: Project Settings: Maps and Modes
commands.description: Sets the default level and game mode the project opens with, both in the editor and in a packaged build. Pointing the game default map at the polished presentation level is an essential step before packaging a client-facing walkthrough.

commands.name: Package Project
commands.description: Compiles and cooks the project into a standalone application, via Platforms > Windows (or another target) > Package Project, that runs without the Unreal Editor. This is how an interactive walkthrough is delivered to a client or marketing suite as a double-clickable build.
